final_answer:
Short answer: under the Guidelines it should not matter which office indicts as far as the guideline range is concerned, so the office that should indict is whichever can first charge the most counts. In practice that means the first office to indict, and ideally the district where venue supports the most (and highest-value) false claims. Neither district's guideline range is inherently higher.

1. Same guideline calculation. Health care fraud under 18 U.S.C. 1347 is sentenced under USSG 2B1.1. Under 1B1.3(a)(2), relevant conduct includes acts that are part of the same course of conduct or common scheme or plan, and fraud offenses are grouped under 3D1.2(d), with loss aggregated. False claims in the other state are therefore counted in the loss figure (and in loss-based and government-health-care-program enhancements such as 2B1.1(b)(1) and (b)(7)) whichever district sentences him, even if those claims are not charged there. Either court should reach roughly the same offense level, so the range is the same.

2. No circuit-law advantage today. South Carolina is in the Fourth Circuit and the Southern District of Georgia is in the Eleventh. They once diverged on whether the commentary's 'intended loss' definition could be used after Kisor v. Wilkie. The Fourth Circuit treated 'loss' as ambiguous and deferred to the commentary (greater of actual or intended loss). The Eleventh Circuit's en banc Dupree decision (57 F.4th 1269) applied Kisor to the commentary. I could not confirm how the Eleventh Circuit then resolved the loss question for 2B1.1. Amendment 827, effective Nov. 1, 2024, moved the loss definition, including intended loss, from the commentary into the guideline text. That removes the split for a sentencing now. This relies on secondary summaries (Welsh & Recker; Eye on Enforcement; USSC primer) that I did not open in full; the Amendment 827 effective date and substance are verified only from those summaries.

3. What actually limits time served is the statutory maximum, not the range. Section 1347 carries up to 10 years per count (20 if serious bodily injury results, life if death). This is stated from knowledge; the Cornell fetch was blocked. A guideline range for a large fraud can exceed one count's maximum. Under 5G1.2(d), the court may stack consecutive sentences across counts to reach the total punishment. So the best indictment is the one with the most counts, and venue controls the counts available. Each office can generally charge only claims submitted, executed or otherwise connected to its own district (Fed. R. Crim. P. 18; Const. art. III, sec. 2 and amend. VI). I did not research venue authority.

4. Sequencing. If both offices indict separately, the second sentencing court must account for the first sentence under 5G1.3. Where the first offense is relevant conduct to the second, 5G1.3(b) requires a concurrent sentence with credit for time served. This undercuts the benefit of a second prosecution. So the offices should not both prosecute the scheme separately. One office should bring the combined case, and the choice should turn on which has venue for more counts. Reasonable alternatives are a single indictment where venue exists in one district for all of the scheme, or the first office to indict, since the second would get largely concurrent time.

Caveat: if the question assumes the offices differ only in guideline treatment, the answer is that neither does. If the intended answer favors one district for another reason (for example, one circuit's rules on relevant conduct or loss), I could not verify one within budget.
